#9803. How to protect WordPress xmlrpc.php and wp-login at the edge

Posted on Nov 21 • Edited on Nov 21 • Originally published at blog.hubfly.space

Bots go straight for /xmlrpc.php and /wp-login.php on every WordPress site they find. Each request wakes PHP and touches your database, even when the guess is wrong. The cheapest defence is to refuse them before they reach WordPress. This guide shows you how to protect WordPress xmlrpc.php and the login page with three edge rules on Hubfly space: block the files WordPress never needs to serve, rate-limit each IP, and keep unfinished or staging sites behind a login. It takes about 15 minutes once the site is running.

Versions used: WordPress 6.9.4 (PHP 8.3, Apache) and MariaDB 11, from the dashboard's WordPress template.

A security plugin runs inside WordPress, so PHP has already started by the time it says no. An edge rule answers before the request reaches your container. On Hubfly space, every project has a Security & Protection Studio between the internet and your containers, and a blocked request is answered there in under a millisecond.

xmlrpc.php deserves special attention: its system.multicall method lets one request try many passwords. Most sites don't use it at all.

In your project, click Create → Compose Stack, search the Presets tab for "wordpress" and click WordPress. It loads two services, wordpress (wordpress:6.9.4-php8.3-apache) and db (mariadb:11), plus two 10 GB volumes, wp-data and db-data.

Both services default to the Dedicated tier (1 vCPU, 1 GB RAM, 5 GB disk each), so read the estimate before you click Deploy Stack. Why: a dedicated container runs all month, and you pay for it all month.

The composer shows $9.10 because it prices the volumes at the Standard rate. Once deployed, the volumes are created as Balanced storage, and the project summary shows $9.21/mo projected. Set a monthly budget cap when you create the project (Advanced Options → Monthly Budget Limit). At 100% of the cap, running workloads are stopped and new deploys are blocked, so you can't overspend by accident.

Click Deploy Stack. The database deploys first, WordPress waits for it, and the whole stack finishes in about a minute and a half. Check that both containers say Running on the canvas, not just that the deploy log says "finished".

Open the wordpress container, go to Network → Add Domain → Auto Endpoint, keep port 80 and click Create Subdomain. You get an HTTPS address like your-site.g.hubfly.app with TLS and Force HTTPS on.

Here's the trap most guides skip: a fresh WordPress container redirects every WordPress page, including the login and xmlrpc.php, to /wp-admin/install.php, and that installer is public. Whoever opens it first creates the admin account. Lock the site before you install it:

Now a request without a Hubfly space session never reaches PHP. A script gets 401, a browser is sent to the sign-in page, and you get through as normal when you're signed in to the dashboard. Finish the WordPress installer in your own browser.

For a staging copy or an internal site, simply leave this on. For a public blog, turn it off once WordPress is installed and use the next two rules instead.

In the WAF Firewall & Logs tab, click Edit Request Filters. Under Blocked Request Paths (Regex / Substring), add these one at a time (press Enter after each):

Click Done, then Save WAF Config at the top right. Nothing is live until you save. Why each one: xmlrpc.php is the brute-force amplifier, .env and .git are the first things scanners probe for, wp-config.php holds your database password, and readme.html announces your WordPress version.

Each entry is matched anywhere in the path as a regular expression, which has useful side effects:

Blocked requests get 403 and a "403 Access blocked" page from the edge.

Don't add /wp-admin or /wp-login.php, even though the docs use /wp-admin as an example. Because the match is a substring, /wp-admin also blocks /wp-admin/admin-ajax.php, which many themes and plugins call for logged-out visitors, and it locks you out of your own dashboard.

Don't rely on the CMS Shield template (under Apply Template) on its own. After applying it, open Edit Request Filters and check that the paths are listed. If the list is empty, add the five entries above by hand.

In the same tab, switch on 2. Rate Limiting. The dialog proposes 10 requests/sec with a burst of 20, using a leaky bucket per client IP (the docs suggest 20 r/s and a burst of 50 as a starting point). Click Apply Settings, then Save WAF Config.

With 10 r/s and a burst of 20, a client that fires 60 requests at once gets about 21 answers and 429 Too Many Requests for the rest, and it's served again a few seconds later. That stops floods and noisy scanners.

Be clear about what it doesn't do. At 10 r/s, one IP can still send 36,000 requests an hour. A patient password guesser stays under any sane limit, so keep a login-limiting plugin such as Limit Login Attempts Reloaded for /wp-login.php.

You want 403, 403, and 200 (or 302 if WordPress isn't installed yet). If Login Required is still on, / returns 401 instead (blocked paths still return 403). That's expected for a staging site. Then scroll down to Security request logs in the studio. Every blocked request is listed there with its status (403, 429 or 401), method, path and client IP.

Is it safe to block xmlrpc.php? For most sites, yes. The block editor, the REST API and normal logins don't use it. Jetpack and some older publishing apps have relied on it, so check yours first.

Does blocking xmlrpc.php stop wp-login brute force? No. It closes the amplified route, but /wp-login.php stays open. Add the per-IP rate limit and a login-limiting plugin.

What status code does a blocked request get? 403 with an "Access blocked" page for blocked paths, 429 when an IP exceeds the rate limit, and 401 for scripts without a session when Login Required is on.

Do the firewall and Identity Access cost extra? No, they're free. You pay only for containers and storage. Creating resources needs a one-time $5 deposit, which stays in your account as credit.

Can I run WordPress on the free tier? You can switch both services to Shared in the composer. Shared containers sleep after 15 minutes without traffic. The 360 free hours a month cover one container that's often asleep, not two that are always on (2 × 730 = 1,460 hours). For a real site, budget for Dedicated.

Related: 502 Bad Gateway in Docker? Bind to 0.0.0.0 · Canary releases with a weighted load balancer

Start free, 360 hours included. Deploy WordPress, lock the installer, and add the three rules above. Try it on Hubfly space

#9801. This fall, reach for this unlikely apple ingredient : Apple cider vinegar is a baker’s secret weapon.

As fall baking season settles in, you're probably reaching for apples — and the many flavor-packed ingredients they produce. Applesauce cooks down into tangy apple butter to be cradled in a flaky galette, while a drop of boiled cider can deliver supercharged apple flavor to crumb cake. But the baking ingredient you may be overlooking may be something you associate more with salad dressings and wellness tonics: apple cider vinegar.

This tangy, apple-y vinegar is a secret ingredient in some of our favorite fall recipes, including cookbook author Claire Saffitz’s Cinnamon-and-Sugar Apple Pie. While lemon juice is the standard acid used in most fruit pie fillings, Claire opts for apple cider vinegar here to complement the filling’s flavors. “It helps as a flavor enhancer, and I also like that it’s apple cider in an apple pie. It’s a nice symmetry,” she mentions.

Similarly, apple cider vinegar is used in the cooking liquid alongside sugar and butter to caramelize apples in a Classic Apple Tarte Tatin. The benefit is twofold: Vinegar’s acidity helps cut the sweetness of the caramel, and it prevents the apples from getting too mushy, instead maintaining their fork-tender texture.

Pastry chef and cookbook author Natasha Pickowicz often leans into the jolt vinegar can add, including adding a few drops to her cake soaks for an additional layer of flavor. “Cake soaks should have a balance of tart, sweet, and savory notes — just like vinaigrette for your favorite salad,” she writes in her cookbook More Than Cake. It can add intrigue to layered cakes like this Golden Spice Cake or Pumpkin Layer Cake. In her cookbook, she also calls for a glaze spiked with apple cider vinegar to brush onto an apple tart after baking. It’s the finishing touch “to further emphasize the tart’s resolute apple-ness,” she writes.

Apple cider vinegar doesn’t need to be limited to only apple desserts, either. In our Old-Fashioned Pecan Pie, we call for apple cider vinegar as a foil to the brown sugar filling’s cloying sweetness. A spoonful of apple cider vinegar may not announce itself boldly, but it makes a small splash for brighter, more balanced bakes.

#9799. Free tier hosting for side projects in 2026: real limits

Posted on Nov 21 • Edited on Nov 21 • Originally published at blog.hubfly.space

Goal: pick a free tier that can run your whole side project, front end, API and database, without it sleeping at the wrong moment or deleting your data after a month. Why it matters: free tier hosting for side projects still exists in 2026, but every free backend now sleeps, caps hours or expires something. The catch you miss is the one that takes your demo down the day someone finally visits it. This guide shows the limits that matter, the hour math nobody does, and what each option costs the day you outgrow it.

These are the plans that run a normal long-lived process: an API, a web app, a bot. Every one of them sleeps, caps usage or needs a card.

Rule of thumb: keep your data in a database whose free tier pauses instead of expiring. A paused Supabase project comes back. A Render free Postgres past its grace period doesn't.

Free tiers are measured in hours, and a month has about 730 hours (744 in a 31-day month). That one number decides whether your free tier actually lasts.

Render, 750 hours per workspace. One service awake all month uses at most 744 hours, so it fits. Two services awake all month need about 1,488 hours. They burn through the allowance around day 15, and then every free service in the workspace is suspended until the 1st.

Neon, 100 CU-hours per project. The free default compute is 0.25 CU. Awake all month: 0.25 × 730 = 182.5 CU-hours, almost double the limit. At 0.25 CU you get 100 ÷ 0.25 = 400 hours, about 16 days of nonstop uptime. Neon's own example, 12 hours a day, uses about 90. So if an uptime pinger keeps your API awake and the API queries the database on every ping, the database stops mid-month.

Hubfly space, 360 hours per account. That's about 12 hours a day for one container, or 24 hours a day for about 15 days. A suspended container stops compute billing. When the account has used all 360 hours, new free containers can't be created until the allowance resets on the 1st, and the dashboard offers to switch to the Dedicated tier instead.

1. Portfolio app with a small API Front end on Cloudflare Pages, API on Render's free instance, data in Neon Free. Nothing expires. The API sleeps after 15 minutes and wakes in about a minute, so put the loading state in the front end.

2. Bot or webhook receiver that runs a few hours a day A small container on the Hubfly space shared tier (0.3 vCPU, 256 MB) or Koyeb's free service. Keep memory low: 256 MB is enough for a small Go, Node or Python process, not for a headless browser.

3. Weekend SaaS experiment with users Front end on Cloudflare Pages, auth and Postgres on Supabase Free. Log in once a week, or the project pauses. Before real users arrive, read the next section.

Free tiers are for learning and demos. The moment someone depends on your app, you want it awake. Here is the cheapest always-on step for one small API plus a managed Postgres database on each platform.

How the Hubfly space numbers add up (730 hours a month): CPU 0.5 × $0.004 × 730 = $1.46, RAM 0.5 GB × $0.002 × 730 = $0.73, storage 4 GB × $0.00001536 × 730 = $0.04. That's $2.23. The managed Postgres Nano size is about $2.02 a month with 10 GiB.

Where others win: Railway is the smoothest jump if you already live there, since $5 covers a small app. Render's 750 free hours can keep one service awake all month for $0 if traffic or a pinger keeps it up (it still spins down after 15 minutes idle), which the 360-hour Hubfly space allowance doesn't. Oracle's Always Free VM gives far more RAM if you're happy running a server yourself. And for a JavaScript-only app, Cloudflare Workers doesn't sleep at all.

It depends on what you host. For files, Cloudflare Pages. For a small API that can sleep, Render's free instance gives 750 hours a month per workspace, enough to keep one service awake all month if traffic or a pinger keeps it up. For a database, Neon Free or Supabase Free, because they pause instead of expiring.

Render (750 hours, sleeps after 15 minutes), Koyeb (one free service, card required), Railway ($1 of usage a month after the trial) and the Hubfly space shared tier (360 hours a month, $5 one-time deposit). Google Cloud Run and Oracle Cloud also have free allowances, but both need a payment method on file.

Oracle Cloud (Always Free Arm VM, 2 OCPUs and 12 GB), Google Cloud (Cloud Run: 180,000 vCPU-seconds and 2 million requests a month) and Cloudflare (Workers: 100,000 requests a day). Oracle and Google Cloud need a card or billing account; Cloudflare's free plan doesn't.

Yes. A free web service spins down after 15 minutes with no inbound traffic and takes about a minute to wake on the next request.

Partly. New accounts get a one-time $5 trial for 30 days. After that, the Free plan gives $1 of usage a month, which doesn't roll over, with 1 project and up to 3 services.

Not for new organizations. Fly.io offers a trial of 2 machine hours or 7 days, whichever comes first. The smallest machine (256 MB) costs $2.19 per 30 days after that.

Yes. Neon Free gives 1 GB per project and scales to zero after 5 minutes. Supabase Free gives 500 MB per project and pauses after a week without activity. Avoid keeping long-term data in Render's free Postgres: it expires after 30 days.

An uptime pinger every few minutes keeps a container awake, but it spends your free hours. On Render, only one service can stay awake all month. Never ping a route that queries your database, or you'll burn the database's compute hours too.

#9798. Benchmarking AWS Amplify, Lambda, Web Functions, and ECS for Next.js

"Should this run on Amplify, Lambda or ECS?" is usually answered with a feature list. I wanted numbers. So I took one Next.js app, deployed it to four AWS runtimes in the same account and Region, including the new Lambda Web Functions, and measured the things that decide the choice in practice: latency under load, cold starts, CPU speed, real limits, and the monthly bill at four traffic levels.

Lambda and ECS run the exact same container image, and the Web Function runs the same files from a .zip. Amplify Hosting builds the same Git commit. Every command, script, and result is in a public repository, with deploy and cleanup steps:

One app, four runtimes, one DynamoDB table:

The app has a few endpoints, each testing something different:

Every response reports which runtime served it, the CPU architecture, and whether it was the first request of that process (a cold start):

Everything runs in eu-central-1. Lambda and Fargate use arm64 (Graviton) and roughly the same size: Lambda with 1024 MB of memory, and a Fargate task with 0.5 vCPU and 1 GB. A Web Function environment has a fixed size of 2 arm64 vCPUs and 2 GB, which you can't change, and Amplify chooses its own compute.

While the setup is running, the only fixed cost is the ECS part: the load balancer, one Fargate task and four public IPv4 addresses, about $1.90 per day. Lambda, Amplify and DynamoDB cost close to nothing at test traffic. Run the cleanup script when you are done.

The app is a normal Next.js app router project. The only special setting is the standalone output, which produces a small self-contained server.js for the container. Amplify builds the app its own way, so the setting is applied only in the Docker build:

The Dockerfile is where Lambda and ECS meet:

--provenance=false keeps a plain single-platform image. By default, buildx adds an attestation manifest and pushes an image index, which Lambda may refuse to use. The script tags each image with the Git commit, so an immutable tag always matches one commit.

Scan on push found one critical CVE on the first push, in zlib from the node:22-alpine base image, not in the app. Base images are rebuilt on a schedule, so security fixes can be days old before they reach the tag you pull. One line in the final stage fixed it:

The next image scanned with zero findings. The compressed image is 88 MB in ECR (233 MB unpacked).

The DynamoDB table is on-demand with one item. Each runtime gets its own IAM role with exactly one permission, dynamodb:GetItem on this table.

A public Function URL now needs both permissions: lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl, and lambda:InvokeFunction limited to calls that come through the URL. I removed the second one to check, and the URL answered with 403 and a helpful message:

A Function URL is free and needs no API Gateway. For production, you would usually put CloudFront in front of it for a custom domain, caching and AWS WAF.

The documented default is 1,000 concurrent executions, but my account had 10. Ten concurrent requests at about 100 ms each is roughly 100 requests per second, and anything above returns 429 Too Many Requests. I requested an increase in Service Quotas (quota code L-B99A9384).

The increase to 1,000 was approved automatically after 2 hours and 20 minutes. Lambda's fast endpoints need far less concurrency than you might expect: at about 40 ms per request, 50 requests per second keep only 2 to 3 environments busy. The CPU endpoint at 50 requests per second peaked at 57 concurrent executions, well over the original limit.

Lambda Web Functions are a new kind of Lambda function for HTTP traffic. Your code is a normal web server that listens on a port, Lambda gives it an HTTPS endpoint, and each execution environment serves many requests at the same time, like a container. It still scales to zero when there is no traffic.

The Next.js standalone server reads HOSTNAME and PORT instead, so the entry file maps one to the other:

To keep the comparison fair, I didn't rebuild the app. The deploy script copies /app out of the same linux/arm64 container image, adds index.js, and deploys that folder:

--include-hidden-files is easy to miss: the Next.js build lives in .next, and without the flag the command leaves hidden folders out of the package. deploy creates the S3 bucket, the function, the first revision and a public endpoint, and waits until the endpoint is active. My first deploy took under a minute.

A revision is an immutable snapshot of code and configuration. Changing an environment variable means a new revision, and an endpoint can route traffic to one revision or split it between two, which gives you canary deployments without CodeDeploy.

The pricing model is different from classic Lambda. In eu-central-1 you pay $0.30 per million requests, $0.000035 per vCPU-second of CPU time that your code actually uses, and $0.0000046 per GB-second of memory for the whole life of each environment. A request that waits for DynamoDB uses almost no CPU, so it costs very little. But an environment that stays alive costs memory time even between requests: one environment kept alive for a month is about $24 in memory alone.

A Fargate task in a private subnet needs a NAT gateway or VPC endpoints to pull its image, and either costs more than the task itself. For this test, the tasks run in public subnets with a public IP, and the security groups do the protecting:

Two roles, two jobs: the execution role lets ECS pull the image and write logs, and the task role is what your code runs as. The DynamoDB permission goes on the task role only.

Two settings save time on every deploy. The target group health check uses /api/health every 10 seconds with a healthy threshold of 2, so a new task gets traffic in about 20 seconds. The deregistration delay is 10 seconds instead of the default 300, so an old task stops quickly.

One bug from my script is worth sharing: --output text separates a list of subnet IDs with tabs, not spaces. My script turned spaces into commas, so the service request got one "subnet ID" with tabs inside and failed with Subnet ID must match subnet-[0-9a-f]+. Pipe the list through tr '\t' ' '.

Amplify Hosting connects to GitHub with its own GitHub App. It does not use an AWS CodeConnections connection, even if you already have one for CodeBuild or CodePipeline. So the first step is in the console: Create new app, GitHub, choose the repository and the main branch. Amplify detects Next.js and uses the amplify.yml from the repository.

This is the biggest surprise for anyone coming from Lambda or ECS. Amplify passes environment variables to the build, not to the server-side code at runtime. The fix is to write the variables your server code needs into .env.production during the build:

The || true is there because my first build failed without it. Before the variables were set, grep found nothing and exited with code 1, and Amplify stopped the build with "Command failed with exit code 1".

Two more rules: variable names can't start with AWS_, so the app reads APP_REGION instead of AWS_REGION, and secrets should not go into .env.production this way, because they end up in the build artifact.

The server-side code needs AWS credentials to call DynamoDB. Amplify calls this a compute role: an IAM role that amplify.amazonaws.com can assume.

Without a compute role, the page renders but the DynamoDB call fails with a credentials error.

The first response from Amplify answered a question the console doesn't:

AWS_LAMBDA_FUNCTION_MEMORY_SIZE is set, so the server code runs on Lambda with 1024 MB, on x64, managed by Amplify. You can't choose the memory size or arm64, and it doesn't count against your account's Lambda concurrency quota.

At 10 requests per second (p50 / p95 / p99 in milliseconds, 1,200 requests each):

On light requests, ECS is the fastest, Lambda and the Web Function are close behind with almost the same medians, and Amplify is about 1.5 times slower than Lambda. ECS wins here because nothing sits between the load balancer and a warm Node.js process.

The CPU row is the surprise. One Fargate task with 0.5 vCPU could not keep up with 10 CPU-heavy requests per second: each request needs about 80 to 150 ms of CPU, so the work arrived faster than half a vCPU could do it. Requests queued, the ALB health checks timed out, and ECS replaced the "unhealthy" task in the middle of the test. 8% of requests failed and the median rose to 1.9 seconds. Lambda, the Web Function and Amplify handled the same load without errors, because they add execution environments as the load grows.

The lesson is not that ECS is slow. A fixed-size service needs auto scaling and headroom, and a health check that shares the CPU with the work it checks can turn an overload into a restart.

At 200 requests per second (p50 / p95 / p99 in milliseconds, 24,000 requests each):

Lambda, the Web Function and Amplify barely noticed the twentyfold increase: their medians moved by a few milliseconds and no request failed. For the Web Function, I ran the 200 requests per second test twice, because AWS says the first load test on a new Web Function scales conservatively, and the table shows the second run. The two runs were within a few milliseconds of each other. Lambda scaled to 234 concurrent executions in the first seconds of the test, then settled between 50 and 90, with zero throttles.

The single ECS task reached 100% CPU and failed. At 50 requests per second the same task used about 65% CPU on the page endpoint, so one 0.5 vCPU task handles roughly 70 page requests per second before it falls over. For real traffic, you would run at least two tasks with target tracking auto scaling at 50 to 60% CPU.

The 50 requests per second results look like the 10 requests per second ones for Lambda, ECS and Amplify, so I left them in the repository instead of adding another table.

One more number explains why Lambda looks so fast: its billed duration (the CloudWatch Duration metric) was 9 to 16 ms at the median for the light endpoints. Most of the 40 ms that the client sees is the network and the Function URL, not your code.

The CPU endpoint does the same 50,000 hashes everywhere:

Lambda gives CPU in proportion to memory: one full vCPU at 1,769 MB. At 1024 MB you get a bit more than half a vCPU, and you pay for the milliseconds you use. A Web Function environment always has 2 vCPUs, and you pay only for the CPU time you use. Node.js runs JavaScript on one thread, so a single request can use only one of them, but that one is a full vCPU. Fargate gives you exactly the vCPU you reserve, all the time, whether you use it or not.

Lambda, 10 forced cold starts (the script changes an environment variable before each request):

Amplify, one request after 20 minutes without traffic, 3 times: 1.94 s, 2.00 s and 0.33 s, compared with about 0.16 s for a warm request. All three were served by a new process, so the third one probably landed on an environment that Amplify had already prepared. You can't see or control this, so plan for about 2 seconds on the first request after a quiet period.

Web Function, 5 forced cold starts (each run creates a new revision, which starts new environments):

ECS has no cold start while a task is running, which is what you pay the fixed monthly price for. Scaling out is a different story: in the ECS events, a replacement task registered with the load balancer about 25 seconds after it started, and then needed two 10-second health checks before it got traffic. A new Lambda environment was ready in about one second.

I asked each runtime to wait longer and longer, and to return larger and larger responses:

If your app has report downloads, file exports or slow third-party calls, these limits decide more than any latency number. Classic Lambda can go beyond 6 MB with response streaming, but that needs code changes. With Web Functions, you get it without changes.

Prices are on-demand prices in eu-central-1 from the AWS Price List API, in November 2026, without free tiers:

Web Functions publish their own usage in CloudWatch (EnvironmentCPUTime, EnvironmentActiveTime and ExecutedRequests in the AWS/Lambda/Web namespace), so I could calculate the real bill for my load tests instead of estimating it:

71% of the bill was memory. At 200 requests per second, Lambda ran up to 55 environments, and none of them served more than 2 requests at the same time (the EnvironmentConcurrentRequests maximum). That was the case in both 200 requests per second runs. AWS documents that a new Web Function starts with a conservative per-environment concurrency limit and raises it as it learns, but I didn't see that happen in about 25 minutes of testing. About 30% of the memory time came after the test, while the environments waited about 5 minutes before Lambda removed them.

The same request mix on classic Lambda would cost about $0.15, or $1.04 per million requests. So in my test, Web Functions cost about four times as much. If the per-environment concurrency grows over time, as AWS describes, this gap will shrink, so treat it as the cost of a new function under a load test, not a final verdict.

For the monthly bill, I used the measured durations: 20 ms of Lambda billed time per request (the 9 to 16 ms median, rounded up), and 5 KB per response. Amplify doesn't publish its billed compute time per request; its CloudWatch Latency metric averaged about 100 ms, which includes the CDN, so I show 100 ms as the upper bound and 30 ms as a likely lower bound. ECS uses the measured capacity of about 50 requests per second per task with headroom. For the Web Function, I used 27 ms of CPU per request, at least one environment alive all month (requests arrive more often than every 5 minutes at these levels), and the measured 0.24 environments per request per second at steady load.

The script is in the repository (bench/cost.py), so you can run it with your own durations and response sizes.

The same build runs on classic Lambda, Web Functions and ECS, so this is not a one-way decision. The Web Function in this article is the same /app folder as the container image, plus a 5-line index.js. Starting on Lambda and moving when your traffic or your limits change is a reasonable path.

The script deletes the Amplify app, the ECS service, cluster, load balancer and target group, the Lambda function, the Web Function and its code versions in the shared awscli-lambdaweb-* bucket, the security groups, the ECR repository, the DynamoDB table, the log groups and the IAM roles. Everything it created has the tag project=runtime-benchmark, so you can check in Tag Editor that nothing is left.

The feature lists told me that ECS is "more powerful", Lambda is "serverless" and Amplify is "easy". The measurements told a more useful story. The always-on container was the fastest per request and the first to fail, because one task is a fixed amount of CPU. The three serverless options were a little slower per request but did not care whether traffic was 10 or 200 requests per second. The newest one, Lambda Web Functions, removes most of classic Lambda's limits and was the fastest on CPU, but its memory billing made it the most expensive serverless option in my test. And the limits that matter most for real apps, request timeout and response size, differ by an order of magnitude between them.

If you only take one thing from this article: measure your own app on the runtime you plan to use, before you choose. The repository makes that a few commands, and the cleanup script removes everything when you are done.

#9797. Ahrefs vs SEMrush: Which SEO Tool Should You Use?


SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

What is SEMrush?


SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Features

  • Most accurate keyword data: Accurate keyword search volume data is crucial for SEO and PPC campaigns by allowing you to identify what keywords are most likely to bring in big sales from ad clicks. SEMrush constantly updates its databases and provides the most accurate data.
  • Largest Keyword database: SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool now features 20-billion keywords, providing marketers and SEO professionals the largest database of keywords.

  • All SEMrush users receive daily ranking data, mobile volume information, and the option to buy additional keywords by default with no additional payment or add-ons needed
  • Most accurate position tracking tool: This tool provides all subscribers with basic tracking capabilities, making it suitable for SEO professionals. Plus, the Position Tracking tool provides local-level data to everyone who uses the tool.
  • SEO Data Management: SEMrush makes managing your online data easy by allowing you to create visually appealing custom PDF reports, including Branded and White Label reports, report scheduling, and integration with GA, GMB, and GSC.
  • Toxic link monitoring and penalty recovery: With SEMrush, you can make a detailed analysis of toxic backlinks, toxic scores, toxic markers, and outreach to those sites.
  • Content Optimization and Creation Tools: SEMrush offers content optimization and creation tools that let you create SEO-friendly content. Some features include the SEO Writing Assistant, On-Page SEO Check, er/SEO Content Template, Content Audit, Post Tracking, Brand Monitoring.

Ahrefs



Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Features

  • Backlink alerts data and new keywords: Get an alert when your site is linked to or discussed in blogs, forums, comments, or when new keywords are added to a blog posting about you.
  • Intuitive interface: The intuitive design of the widget helps you see the overall health of your website and search engine ranking at a glance.
  • Site Explorer: The Site Explorer will give you an in-depth look at your site's search traffic.
  • Domain Comparison
  • Reports with charts and graphs
  • JavaScript rendering and a site audit can identify SEO issues.
  • A question explorer that provides well-crafted topic suggestions

Direct Comparisons: Ahrefs vs SEMrush

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

User Interface

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

AHREFS



The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

  • You can see analytics from the dashboard, including search engine rankings to domain ratings, referring domains, and backlink
  • Jumping from one tool to another is easy. You can use the Keyword Explorer to find a keyword to target and then directly track your ranking with one click.
  • The website offers a tooltip helper tool that allows you to hover your mouse over something that isn't clear and get an in-depth explanation.

SEMRUSH



When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

You'll also find some other options like

  • A search bar allows you to enter a domain, keyword, or anything else you wish to explore.
  • A menu on the left side of the page provides quick links to relevant information, including marketing insights, projects, keyword analytics, and more.
  • The customer support resources located directly within the dashboard can be used to communicate with the support team or to learn about other resources such as webinars and blogs.
  • Detailed descriptions of every resource offered. This detail is beneficial for new marketers, who are just starting.

WHO WINS?

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

Rank Tracking

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

Ahrefs



The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRUSH



SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

All subscribers are given regular data updates and mobile search rankings upon subscribing

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

WHO WINS?

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment.

Keyword Research

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

AHREFS



The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

  • It can search multiple keywords in a single search and analyze them together. At SEMrush, you also have this feature in Keyword Overview.
  • Ahrefs has a variety of keywords for different search engines, including Google, YouTube, Amazon, Bing, Yahoo, Yandex, and other search engines.
  • When you click on a keyword, you can see its search volume and keyword difficulty, but also other keywords related to it, which you didn't use.

SEMRUSH



SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear.

The Keyword Magic Tool also lets you to:

  • Show performance metrics by keyword
  • Search results are based on both broad and exact keyword matches.
  • Show data like search volume, trends, keyword difficulty, and CPC.
  • Show the first 100 Google search results for any keyword.
  • Identify SERP Features and Questions related to each keyword
  • SEMrush has released a new Keyword Gap Tool that uncovers potentially useful keyword opportunities for you, including both paid and organic keywords.

WHO WINS?

Both of these tools offer keyword research features and allow users to break down complicated tasks into something that can be understood by beginners and advanced users alike.

If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations.

Competitor Analysis

Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you.

AHREFS



Ahrefs' domain comparison tool lets you compare up to five websites (your website and four competitors) side-by-side.it also shows you how your site is ranked against others with metrics such as backlinks, domain ratings, and more.

Use the Competing Domains section to see a list of your most direct competitors, and explore how many keywords matches your competitors have.

To find more information about your competitor, you can look at the Site Explorer and Content Explorer tools and type in their URL instead of yours.

SEMRUSH



SEMrush provides a variety of insights into your competitors' marketing tactics. The platform enables you to research your competitors effectively. It also offers several resources for competitor analysis including:

Traffic Analytics helps you identify where your audience comes from, how they engage with your site, what devices visitors use to view your site, and how your audiences overlap with other websites.

SEMrush's Organic Research examines your website's major competitors and shows their organic search rankings, keywords they are ranking for, and even if they are ranking for any (SERP) features and more.

The Market Explorer search field allows you to type in a domain and lists websites or articles similar to what you entered. Market Explorer also allows users to perform in-depth data analytics on These companies and markets.

WHO WINS?

SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition.

Pricing

Ahrefs

  • Lite Monthly: $99/month
  • Standard Monthly: $179/month
  • Annually Lite: $990/year
  • Annually Standard: $1790/year

SEMRUSH

  • Pro Plan: $119.95/month
  • Guru Plan:$229.95/month
  • Business Plan: $449.95/month

Which SEO tool should you choose for digital marketing?

When it comes to keyword data research, you will become confused about which one to choose.

Consider choosing Ahrefs if you

  • Like friendly and clean interface
  • Searching for simple keyword suggestions

  • Want to get more keywords for different search engines like Amazon, Bing, Yahoo, Yandex, Baidu, and more

 

Consider SEMrush if you:

  • Want more marketing and SEO features
  • Need competitor analysis tool
  • Need to keep your backlinks profile clean
  • Looking for more keyword suggestions for Google

Both tools are great. Choose the one which meets your requirements and if you have any experience using either Ahrefs or SEMrush let me know in the comment section which works well for you.

#9795. How to Choose an AI Subscription by Task, Budget, and Region

Most people pick an AI plan backwards. They start with a product name, then try to justify the spend. It works better the other way: write down what you actually do, how often you do it, and how much you will pay each month. Only then look at official plan names.

This article uses consumer plan names and list prices from vendor pages checked on 22 November 2026 (UTC+9). Prices move, and they can differ by country, billing cycle, and promotional offers. If a number below could not be read clearly from the official page, it is omitted.

Write a short list of recurring tasks, not a wish list. A few examples:

Frequency matters as much as the task type. Occasional use and daily heavy use are different purchasing problems. If you only need a model for a one-off experiment, start on a free tier and stop there if it is enough.

Personal subscriptions and developer APIs should be decided separately. OpenAIâ€™s own pricing docs state that API-key sessions use API pricing, not the included allowance on a ChatGPT plan. Anthropic likewise sells Claude as a consumer/team product and as a platform with token rates. Buying a personal membership does not automatically give you equivalent API credit.

Decide a monthly ceiling in the currency you will actually be billed in, then compare official list prices against that ceiling. Entering zero as a budget is a useful test: it forces you to try free options first.

On 22 November 2026, these individual list prices were published on official pages:

ChatGPT (from OpenAIâ€™s Codex/ChatGPT pricing docs and the ChatGPT pricing page):

The public pricing page also lists Business and Enterprise (Business starts at two users). Paid personal plans are priced per user per month; Business and Enterprise also have annual billing options, according to the FAQ on the pricing page.

Claude (from Claudeâ€™s plans and pricing page, reached via anthropic.com/pricing):

Google AI plans (from Google Oneâ€™s Google AI plans page):

The Google page was also showing a limited-time promotional discount on 22 November 2026. I have not treated that discount as the standard price. The list price for Google AI Plus was not clearly readable in the extracted page text, so it is not quoted here.

These are list prices, not a ranking. A $20 plan is not â€œbetterâ€ than an $8 plan if your tasks fit the cheaper one.

Plan pages describe access, not a guarantee that you will never hit a cap. ChatGPTâ€™s help article says Plus may still have usage limits, especially when demand is high. Claudeâ€™s Pro and Max pages describe usage multiples and, on some plans, five-hour windows; Ultra is described as having no five-hour limit. Read the current feature list on the official page for the exact plan, because model names change.

A practical mapping, based only on what those pages claim:

If you need an API, open the vendorâ€™s API pricing page and budget for tokens separately. Do not treat a personal Plus or Pro invoice as API credit.

Availability is not the same as â€œthe website loads.â€ Google, for example, publishes separate country lists for different Gemini and Google One products. A plan that exists in the United States may be offered later, or not at all, in another market. Payment profile, account type (personal vs work/school), and age rules can also block checkout even when the product page is visible.

If a vendor says a product is not available in your country, treat that as an eligibility question, not a prompt to change region unofficially. For Gemini and Google AI plans specifically, Maihaoâ€™s English guide Gemini not available in your country walks through checking the official country list and the exact product that rejected the signup.

When you compare plans, use the same region and currency you will pay in. A US list price can be a poor guide to what a local checkout shows.

If you want a structured checklist rather than a spreadsheet of your own, the free AI Subscription Advisor lets you choose tasks, a monthly budget (use 0 to prefer free options), region, and required capabilities, then compares recommendations with limitations and verification dates. It does not require an account. It is a helper for matching needs to published plan facts, not a substitute for the vendor checkout page.

Before you pay, open the official plan page again. If a price or model name in any article â€” including this one â€” disagrees with the checkout screen, trust the checkout screen.

#9793. Six Password Reset Vulnerabilities and How to Prevent Them

Autonomous security testing powered by AI agents. Powerful. Accurate. Actionable. hackerme.ai

Autonomous security testing powered by AI agents. Powerful. Accurate. Actionable. hackerme.ai

Autonomous security testing powered by AI agents. Powerful. Accurate. Actionable. hackerme.ai

This is an example, not a report from a customer. Imagine a support inbox: someone never asked for a password reset, but they received a "your password was changed" email, and now their login no longer works. Their old password was long and unique. Nobody guessed it.

Nobody needed to. A reset flow is a way into an account without the current password, by design. A valid reset link may let whoever holds it set a new password. Whether that is enough to take the account depends on other controls: a second factor at the reset step, a prompt to re-authenticate, a notification the real owner sees in time, session invalidation after the change, or a token that has already expired or been used.

OWASP calls this functionality "a common source of vulnerabilities" even though it "looks straightforward and easy to implement" (OWASP Forgot Password Cheat Sheet). The usual weak points sit at six places in the flow. Run the active tests only on systems you own or have written permission to test.

When someone types an address into "Forgot password", the response should not reveal whether an account exists. OWASP's Authentication Cheat Sheet lists "We just sent you a password reset link" and "This email address doesn't exist in our database" as incorrect responses, and gives the correct one: "If that email address is in our database, we will send you an email to reset your password" (OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet).

The message is the easy part. The Forgot Password Cheat Sheet also asks for responses that "return in a consistent amount of time," for example by sending the email asynchronously instead of exiting early for unknown addresses. A page that answers in a few milliseconds for unknown addresses and noticeably later for real ones tells an attacker the same thing as a different message.

Then rate-limit the endpoint. OWASP recommends per-account rate limiting or a CAPTCHA, because otherwise an attacker can flood a user's inbox. Return the same 429 Too Many Requests whether or not the account exists (RFC 6585, section 4), or the limiter itself becomes an enumeration oracle. Do not lock the account: OWASP notes that a forgotten-password attack should not produce a lockout, because that lets anyone deny access to users whose names they know.

Many frameworks make it easy to build an absolute URL from "the current host". In a reset email, that convenience is the vulnerability. PortSwigger describes password reset poisoning: an attacker submits a reset request for the victim with a Host header pointing at a domain they control, the site sends a genuine token, and the link inside points at the attacker. If the victim clicks it, or a mail scanner fetches it, the token is delivered to the attacker (PortSwigger: Password reset poisoning).

OWASP's instruction is direct: "Don't rely on the Host header while creating the reset URLs." Use one configured HTTPS base URL per environment, and reject host names you do not serve. Treat X-Forwarded-Host the same way: trust it only from your own proxy.

OWASP lists the properties every reset token needs: generated with a cryptographically secure random number generator, long enough to resist brute force, linked to an individual user, invalidated after use, stored securely, and expiring after an appropriate period.

Here is a minimal sketch in Python that follows those properties. It is something to adapt, not a drop-in library.

secrets.token_urlsafe(32) uses Python's module for security tokens, which documents 32 bytes (256 bits) of randomness as sufficient for the typical case (Python docs: secrets). Never use random, timestamps, user IDs or sequential values. Store only a hash, so a leaked database does not contain working links. For a long random token, a fast hash such as SHA-256 is a reasonable choice; slow password hashing is meant for secrets people choose (OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet). Issuing a new token should burn older ones for that user. An expired, used or unknown token should produce the same generic error page.

The sketch is single-process and in-memory. In a real application, two requests can redeem the same token at once, so marking it used must be one atomic database operation that succeeds only if it changes exactly one unused, unexpired row.

The token sits in a URL, and URLs travel.

OWASP asks reset pages to send Referrer-Policy: no-referrer. When no policy is set, browsers default to strict-origin-when-cross-origin, which sends only the origin on cross-origin requests (MDN: Referrer-Policy). A missing header is not proof that the token leaks to third parties in current browsers. It is a missing layer: the default still sends the full URL on same-origin requests, and a looser policy elsewhere on the site would apply.

Analytics, chat widgets and session-replay tools on the reset page can read location.href. The cleanest pattern is a reset page with no third-party scripts. Mail scanners can also open the link before the user does. If a GET burns the single-use token, the real user may find it "already used". Show the form on GET, and consume the token only on POST.

If an attacker already had a session, a new password alone does not remove them. OWASP recommends invalidating existing sessions, or asking the user whether to do so, and advises against signing the user in automatically after the reset. The Session Management Cheat Sheet lists a completed password change among the events that should require reauthentication (OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet).

Send a notification that the password was changed, without the password in it, as OWASP recommends. In the example above, that email is what turned a silent change into a support ticket. Include a way to report "this wasn't me" that does not depend on the account's current password.

Use two test accounts you control, and staging where possible. We have not run the commands below against a live site.

Submit the form for a real test address and for an address that does not exist, and compare status, visible message, size and timing. You want the same status and message for both. A "no such user" error is a leak. Small size differences can come from a CSRF token; timing needs many requests before it means anything.

In staging, send the same request with a foreign Host (and again with X-Forwarded-Host) and read the email that arrives. If the link points at the foreign host, that header is being trusted. A 404 or 421 from the proxy only shows that this request was refused; read the link-building code as well.

With a test account, reuse a spent link, use the older of two links, wait past expiry, and open the page with GET before submitting the form. The last check shows whether a GET burns the token. Look at the reset page for Referrer-Policy and third-party scripts. After a reset, a second browser that was already signed in should be signed out or asked to authenticate again.

If every step behaved as intended for these test accounts, this flow did what you asked when you tested it. Other recovery paths, and the difference between staging and production, still need their own review.

We are the HackerMe team, and we build a free scanner for public pages and headers. It cannot read reset emails or token storage.

#9791. What AWS Emulator lets you test before you deploy

Posted on Nov 21 • Originally published at artificialcuriositylabs.ai

AWS Emulator lets you test code that calls AWS without deploying it first. AWS made it generally available on November 11, 2026. It runs on your machine or in continuous integration (CI), where it accepts supported API calls from the AWS CLI and SDKs. You don't need an AWS account to run it.

Use it to test the AWS behavior your application depends on: can it read a file from S3, reject a duplicate write in DynamoDB, or recover when SQS delivers a message twice? Run those checks on a laptop while you change the code, repeat them on pull requests, or let a coding agent test its changes without access to a live account. Coverage varies by operation, so start with the behavior you need to verify.

Point your CLI or SDK at the emulator's local HTTPS endpoint. When a test creates a bucket, uploads a file, and reads it back, each call sees the state left by the previous one. The emulator keeps that state in memory and discards it on exit, so a fresh instance gives the next test run a clean set of resources.

The CLI is handy for creating fixtures and inspecting results. The SDK lets the application use its regular clients. AWS provides Linux packages and a Docker setup for macOS and Windows, and Rust tests can embed the emulator directly. In server mode the emulator generates its own signing credentials and local certificate. It doesn't need access to your AWS account to serve requests.

There's a useful distinction between configuring a service and using it. Creating an S3 bucket is a control-plane operation; uploading and reading an object are data-plane operations. A successful create call can mean the emulator accepted the configuration and recorded it. It tells you much less about whether the workload behind it will run. In one public CDK test, the emulator created an ECS service record, yet no containers started. The right test depends on which of those two outcomes the application needs.

Start with the AWS operations your code calls. A broad list of services can tell you what to investigate; a passing test of the behavior you depend on tells you what to keep in the local test suite.

There are public examples at both ends of that range. A notes app backed by S3 and DynamoDB covers save, read, overwrite, and missing notes and includes a GitHub Actions workflow. A serverless order demo exercises payment retries and inventory rollback. Its author also hit runtime and integration gaps. Copy the test idea; verify the operations on the release you plan to use.

AWS calls the match between its services and the emulator fidelity. The release scores count test cases that match AWS, including expected errors and resulting state. A service score is not the percentage of API operations implemented. List your calls, look for matching cases in the fidelity test suite, and run your own workflow against the pinned release. An unimplemented operation returns 501 Not Implemented; a successful response is a reason to check the actual state or side effect you care about.

Start the emulator, point the SDK or CLI at its loopback address, and use the generated credentials and certificate. The connection guide has the environment settings. Run setup and tests in the same isolated process, with real AWS credentials removed. Verify where requests go before allowing writes. A reported JavaScript SQS setup sent CreateQueue to the emulator but let SendMessage follow the returned queue URL to AWS. Checking only the initial endpoint would have missed that.

For a concrete example, I tested a worker that reads a file from S3 and records its metadata in DynamoDB. The queue message carries the file key and an application request ID. I let the first write succeed, then prevented the worker from acknowledging the delivery:

The second delivery had the same message ID and a new SQS receipt handle. That handle identifies a delivery and is needed to acknowledge it. The worker uses the application request ID to identify the work. A conditional write keyed by that ID left exactly one unchanged record. That verifies the worker's response to redelivery; managed Lambda polling still needs a separate test.

AWS's coding-agent setup skill can start the emulator, connect the SDK or CLI, and check which operations a project uses. The launch walkthrough shows a coding agent creating a DynamoDB table, writing an item, and reading it back. Give the agent an expected outcome it can assert, not merely a service it can call:

List the AWS operations this change touches. Use a fresh, pinned emulator and synthetic data. Reproduce one failure, then verify the exact state left behind. Report what passed locally and what still needs real AWS. Do not deploy.

That loop also works when the application under development happens to be an AI agent. Test the S3 or DynamoDB calls behind its tools locally. Verify model tool selection, hosted runtime behavior, and permissions in staging. Those are different tests from the ones the coding agent runs while editing the project.

There's a second agent story in the emulator itself. AWS says agents build and maintain it: they find differences from real AWS, write tests and fixes, and send changes through a release pipeline that reruns the fidelity tests. The part worth copying is the independent check. An agent can propose the code and even write the test, but the expected behavior needs a reference outside the agent's own implementation.

I'd use AWS Emulator as a pull-request check for code that reads or changes AWS state. The SQS test is the reason: I could reproduce the missed acknowledgement, inspect the second delivery, and verify the exact record left behind. That is stronger evidence than a mock configured to return the response I expected, and I didn't have to deploy the worker to get it.

Start with one assertion a caller would notice: one record after two deliveries, an unchanged item after a conflict, or a message arriving in the intended queue. Keep a small real-AWS suite for the documented limits: permissions, account and Region boundaries, and the managed behavior your application relies on. Use real infrastructure for performance tests.

For coding agents, this is a step toward a better division of work. Let them prototype, build, and verify changes against disposable resources, then hand over the evidence. Operating a live system calls for separate controls: narrowly scoped permissions, a record of what the agent did, approval for consequential changes, and a way to roll them back. A passing local test earns a staging run; it doesn't grant production access.

The open question is how long a local test and its staging counterpart keep answering the same question. When the emulator, SDK, or service changes, which small set of workflows is worth running in both places to catch drift?

#9790. AI Made Us Faster. So Why Do Designers Have Less Time?

Art director and brand designer. Ex-Avito, ivi, MY.GAMES. Founder of Design Warm-ups, a 3,000+ designer community.

Art director and brand designer. Ex-Avito, ivi, MY.GAMES. Founder of Design Warm-ups, a 3,000+ designer community.

Art director and brand designer. Ex-Avito, ivi, MY.GAMES. Founder of Design Warm-ups, a 3,000+ designer community.

A poster that used to take me a day now takes a minute to generate. Last night I built an animated website in one evening without writing a single line of code. By every estimate, designers should have half their lives back.

Yet I haven't met a single designer who has more free time. Deadlines are shorter, revisions are longer, and by the evening there are so many options that your eyes start to blur.

So I tried to figure out what is going on. Are we bad at working with AI? Were we sold a fantasy? Or is this just a bubble that is about to pop? The answer turned out to be more interesting than all three.

In 2025, researchers at METR ran a simple experiment. Sixteen experienced developers worked on real tasks, some with AI tools and some without. Before they started, they expected AI to make them 24% faster.

With AI, tasks took 19% longer. The strangest part: even after the experiment, they believed AI had made them 20% faster.

The study is small, and it is about developers, not designers. But the same picture shows up in much larger surveys:

2,500 workers and executives in 4 countries

96% of executives expect AI to raise productivity. 77% of employees say it added to their workload

52 interviews, 300+ public AI initiatives

95% of organizations got zero return from generative AI

Computers went through the same thing in the 1980s. Economist Robert Solow famously observed that you could see the computer age everywhere except in the productivity statistics. The growth did come, but only after people rebuilt the way they worked.

I see three reasons, and none of them is that the models are bad.

1. Generation got cheap. Choosing didn't. A designer used to make three options and bring the best one. Now you can get 200 in an hour. Each one has to be looked at, compared, and rejected for a reason. Nobody counts that time, but it eats all the savings.

2. Clients know generation takes a minute too. So "by Friday" turned into "by tomorrow", and one round of revisions turned into five. Economists call this the Jevons paradox: when something gets cheaper, we consume more of it. Cheap images didn't reduce the work. They increased the appetite.

3. We dropped AI into the old process. Brief, references, sketches, approvals all stayed the same. There is just a new "generate" button in the middle. According to Upwork, 47% of employees using AI don't know how to reach the productivity gains their managers expect. And in the MIT report, the 5% of companies that succeeded rebuilt the process itself instead of buying one more tool.

There is one more thing METR showed. With AI, the feeling of speed and actual speed drift apart. Generating gives you the sense that work is happening even when it is stuck. For designers, it looks like an hour of rerolling one frame instead of five minutes thinking about what exactly is wrong with it.

Fair question. In June 2026, JPMorgan estimated global AI infrastructure spending at $5.5 trillion through 2030. The largest cloud providers alone are spending about $650 billion in 2026, increasingly with borrowed money. Investors argue about one thing: whether demand will catch up with the spending.

For designers, I think something else matters more. Even if the financial bubble pops, the tools won't disappear. After the dot-com crash in 2000, the internet didn't go away. The companies that couldn't make money on it did, and the ones that could grew in their place.

AI looks similar. If there is a bubble, it is in expectations: "buy a subscription and everything gets faster." The data above shows it doesn't work that way. But the change in the profession has already happened, and it won't roll back.

There is another tension in the industry. Open Threads and it looks like everyone is a designer now. The profession has ballooned and is changing in front of us. But behind a lot of those generations is a lack of basics: composition, grids, typography. AI doesn't fix that. It mass-produces it.

That is especially true for product designers moving from interfaces into visual work. A component library keeps a UI consistent, but there is no Storybook for light, texture and framing.

None of these steps requires a new model. They are all about who is running the process.

We weren't fooled. We were sold faster execution and assumed we had bought faster work. AI speeds up making things. It doesn't free up a designer's time on its own. The person who frees up time is the one who decided in advance what they are making and knows how to choose quickly.

That animated website from the first paragraph took one evening for exactly that reason: I knew what feeling I wanted before I typed the first prompt. Without that, I would still be rerolling it.

Has AI saved you time, or eaten it? And how have your deadlines changed in the last year?

AI Didn’t Kill Design. But Something About the Profession Is Changing Anyway

Art director and brand designer. Ex-Avito, ivi, MY.GAMES. Founder of Design Warm-ups, a 3,000+ designer community.

#9788. Why asking AI to rate your product doesn't work (and what does)

If you have ever pasted a product idea into ChatGPT or Claude and asked "would people buy this? rate it 1 to 5", you probably got a 4. Try a different idea and you will probably get a 4 again, or a 3.

That is not because every idea is decent. It is because language models play it safe when you ask them for a number. A 2025 paper measured this properly, and found a fix that is surprisingly simple.

The paper is LLMs Reproduce Human Purchase Intent via Semantic Similarity Elicitation of Likert Ratings (arXiv 2510.08338), by researchers at PyMC Labs and Colgate-Palmolive.

They had real data from 57 product concept surveys, with 9,300 people. Each person saw a personal care product concept and answered "How likely are you to purchase the product?" on a 1 to 5 scale.

Then they asked LLMs the same question, with each LLM playing one of the real respondents (same age, income, location and so on), and compared the results.

When the model was asked to reply with a number from 1 to 5, the average looked reasonable, but the spread was wrong. Almost every answer was a 3 or a 4. Real people use the whole scale.

The paper measures this with KS similarity, where 1.0 means the spread of ratings is identical to the real one. Asking for a number directly scored 0.26.

The method that worked is called Semantic Similarity Rating (SSR):

The result is not one guessed number but a probability for every rating. The answer above might come out as 8% for 1, 34% for 2, 30% for 3, 20% for 4 and 8% for 5: it leans towards "no", with some uncertainty, which is how a real person feels about it.

With this method the KS similarity went from 0.26 to 0.88, and the ranking of products reached about 90% of human test-retest reliability. That last number means it agreed with real results nearly as well as real people agree with themselves when they take the same survey twice.

I turned the method into an open-source agent skill that works in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Google Antigravity and Gemini CLI:

https://github.com/AryamanSi17/synthetic-consumer-research

There is also a free demo where you can type a customer answer and see the rating probabilities: https://huggingface.co/spaces/AryamanSi/semantic-similarity-rating-demo

Use it as a fast first filter: ranking two or three concepts, testing a price, or finding the objections you had not thought of. Before you spend money on a real panel, it costs a few cents and a few minutes.

Do not use it as a replacement for real customers on big decisions. The method was validated on US personal care products. Other categories, countries and languages are less tested, and the model only knows what was in its training data.

If you have real survey data, you can check how close the synthetic survey gets with the --human option, which is the best way to calibrate it for your market.

Paper: Maier, Aslak, Fiaschi et al. (2025), arXiv:2510.08338. Official reference implementation: pymc-labs/semantic-similarity-rating.
